newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Asean rejects trade and labour standards link.
newsitem.headline: Asean rejects trade and labour standards link.

text.p: Labour ministers from ASEAN member countries reaffirmed their stand against linking labour conditions to international trading rules, Vietnamese Labour Minister Tran Dinh Hoan said on Wednesday.

"There should not be any...link between labour standards and economic and trade issues," Hoan told Reuters after a meeting in Hanoi of labour ministers from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN). "And we reached a consensus on that."
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

Hoan said the ministers, who met behind closed doors on Tuesday, wanted to reaffirm their position in a dispute which took centre stage at a World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting in December.

The United States and other Western nations have argued that international trade rules should be used to raise Third World labour standards, eradicate sweatshops and stop an estimated 250 million children from working, often in appalling conditions.
Backed by France and Canada, Washington has said it wants the issue to be thrashed out at the WTO, which has its own court to resolve trade disputes.
Other countries, mostly from the developing world, argue that the United States is trying to protect jobs at home from cheap Third World labour.

At the WTO conference in Singapore, member countries agreed to observe "internationally recognised core labour standards", confirming that the International Labour Organisation (ILO) was "the competent body to set and deal" with them.
Both sides in the argument went away from that meeting proclaiming vistory.

Vietnam's official media, in reports on the ASEAN ministers' informal meeting in Hanoi, said it had been agreed that the ILO was "the only world agency responsible for setting labour standards -- not the WTO".

Hoan said the ASEAN ministers did not discuss U.S. President Bill Clinton's recent endorsement of an apparel industry pact aimed at curbing the use of child labour and other sweatshop conditions at overseas factories used by U.S. firms.
Recently, U.S. sportswear firm Nike Inc came under fire following allegations of labour abuse at a factory near Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City which is operated by a Taiwanese subcontractor.
